1.2 — The Unity Editor Tour

Before you write a line of code you need to read the tool that runs everything. Unity is five windows, one Inspector, and a trap called play mode. Ten minutes of tour saves ten hours of confusion — and along the way you will discover something strange about the Player in this project.

Tour ~20 min

Open the Overworld scene. Find and name all five panes:

PaneWhat it showsYour move
Hierarchy (left)Every GameObject in this scene, as a treeClick things. Some are parents with children — why?
Scene (centre)The world, editable from aboveScroll to zoom, right-drag to pan, F to focus
GameWhat the camera sees when you press PlaySwitch back and forth with the tabs
Inspector (right)Everything about the selected object — as componentsSelect the Player and read the whole list
Project (bottom)The repo's actual files: Scenes, Scripts, Prefabs, ArtworkNavigate to Assets/Scripts and find PlayerController.cs

The one idea to remember: a GameObject is an empty container, and components are the abilities you bolt onto it. Select the Player in the Hierarchy and expand its children. This is everything it has:

ObjectComponentWhat it does here
Player
(tagged Player)		 Transform Position, rotation, and scale — every GameObject has one
Player Controller (Script) Nothing yet. Select it and count the fields: there are none. It is an empty shell waiting for you.
(no Sprite Renderer here) The Player itself is invisible. Keep reading.
Sprite
(a child of Player)		 Transform Position relative to its parent — this is why children move with their parent
Sprite Renderer What you actually see on screen — the picture of your character
Animator The idle animation that plays when you press Play
Why is the picture on a child object? This is a very common Unity pattern. The parent Player is the thing you move, collide, and track. The child Sprite is just the artwork hanging off it. Keep this split in mind — in a few lessons, finding components on children rather than on the root will matter a great deal.

Tinker: Take the player apart

In the Overworld scene, select the Player. Press Play after each change, and undo with Ctrl+Z when you stop:

  1. Select the child Sprite object and untick its Animator. What happens to the animation? What does that prove about which object is responsible for what you see?
  2. Select the parent Player and untick the Player Controller component. Press Play and try to move. What changes — and why is that the answer?
  3. The Player object has no Sprite Renderer of its own. Where must that component live for your character to be visible, and what does that tell you about how the two objects relate?
  4. Drag the Player to a completely different spot in the Scene view while not playing. Which numbers changed in the Transform component?
The Trap ~15 min
Play mode is a dream, edit mode is reality. Press Play. While the game runs, drag a Coin prefab from Assets/Prefabs into the scene. Stop the game. The coin is gone. Everything you change in play mode — positions, Inspector values, even new objects — evaporates when you press stop. Students lose whole afternoons to this every year. You will lose five minutes once, and never again.

See it happen: press Play, select the Player, and change Transform Position X to 15 in the Inspector. Your character teleports across the screen. Press stop. Where is the Player now, and where did your change go?

The safe version of that workflow: change values in play mode to experiment and test, then stop and enter the winning numbers in edit mode so they persist. For the rest of the year this is your primary live-tuning workflow — you will use it in the very next lesson to find a movement speed that feels right.

Socratic

  1. Why would Unity be designed so that play-mode changes vanish? Think about testing an idea fifty times a day — what does "reset to the last known good game" buy you?
  2. Unticking the Player Controller changed nothing at all. What does that tell you about the relationship between a component and the code inside it?
  3. Is play mode closer to a save-file system or to an undo button, and why?
Ship It ~10 min

One more piece of housekeeping: scenes are files like anything else. When you move something in the Overworld, the .unity file is dirty — Ctrl+S saves the scene (look for the asterisk in the tab). Save, then commit and push: "1.2: editor tour".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name all five panes and what each one is for
  • Explain "GameObject = container, components = abilities" using the Player as the example
  • Point at which object carries the Sprite Renderer and which carries the script
  • Demonstrate play-mode vanishing with your own two hands
  • Save a scene and commit + push the change
